projects.rationale: Activist Handbook demonstrates strong nonprofit, community-driven governance, explicit service to grassroots and underserved activist communities, real-world adoption and international use, a genuine open contribution model, and a collaborative, participatory approach, with only minor deduction for partial (not full) open source status.

Adhocracy+ demonstrates strong alignment with participatory democracy and nonprofit governance, provides open source code with active development, serves municipal residents and public administrations with evidence of real-world use, but is limited by single-organization governance and lacks explicit evidence of environmental sustainability.

AISafety.info demonstrates nonprofit governance and some open contribution, but lacks evidence of deep community ownership, user-centred design for marginalized groups, or strong real-world adoption, resulting in a middling score under a governance- and justice-focused evaluation.

Alaveteli strongly aligns with the evaluative constitution by providing an open-source, nonprofit, citizen-focused platform for FOI requests with international adoption, transparent governance, and a clear commitment to participatory democracy and accountability.

Aleph (OCCRP) demonstrates strong nonprofit governance, serves investigative journalists and civil society with open source infrastructure, is widely adopted with proven impact, and embodies collaborative, public-interest technology, though heavy US government funding introduces some governance risk.

AlgorithmWatch demonstrates strong nonprofit governance, a focus on algorithmic justice for marginalised and general populations, real-world adoption across Europe, partial open source practices, and a collaborative, advocacy-driven approach, though its open source commitment is not fully comprehensive.

All Our Ideas demonstrates strong nonprofit governance, a participatory and citizen-focused design, real-world government adoption, open source commitment, collaborative features, and direct impact on democratic participation, with only minor uncertainty around environmental sustainability.

This nonprofit publication is transparently governed as a project of a larger organization with no evidence of founder profit, but it primarily serves professional and institutional users, lacks open source or community ownership, and provides little evidence of direct impact on underserved populations or collaborative/cooperative governance.

Anna's Archive demonstrates strong user-centred design for underserved populations and genuine open source commitment, but lacks evidence of transparent or participatory governance, and its governance appears individual rather than community-based.

Landlord Tech Watch demonstrates strong grassroots governance, serves marginalized tenants and advocates, is open source with active contributions, and has real-world academic impact, though evidence of direct tenant adoption and collaborative governance specifics is limited.

Aragon demonstrates partial community governance and open-source practices with real-world adoption in the DAO space, but its VC-backed LLC structure, partial community ownership, and lack of clear focus on underserved populations or public health limit its alignment with the progressive evaluative constitution.

arXiv demonstrates transparent, grant-funded academic governance, serves a global community of researchers and students, is widely adopted, and embodies open access ideals, though its open source status is only partial and it is not explicitly cooperative or environmentally focused.

This is a theoretical academic framework with no evidence of real-world adoption, user-centred design for underserved populations, or genuine open source/community governance, but it is structurally focused on participatory democracy and governance, warranting a modest score for conceptual alignment.

Atlas of Surveillance scores highly for nonprofit governance, serving citizens and advocacy groups, real-world adoption in policy and advocacy, partial open source, and collaborative community data collection, though it is less strong on environmental sustainability and full open governance.

Bellingcat's toolkit is a nonprofit, transparently funded, open source platform serving investigative and citizen journalists—an underserved, globally relevant community—with clear evidence of real-world adoption, collaborative features, and strong governance, though lacking explicit environmental sustainability features.

The project is a nonprofit tool serving low-income and marginalized UK citizens with real-world adoption and social impact, but lacks evidence of open source, community ownership, or collaborative governance.

Kagi SlopStop demonstrates real-world adoption and some collaborative, user-driven features, but its for-profit structure, partial open source, and focus on general rather than underserved users limit its alignment with participatory, justice-oriented values.

Bonfire exemplifies cooperative governance, open source commitment, user-centric design for marginalized digital communities, and real-world adoption, with only minor deductions for early-stage adoption and sustainability challenges.

Bluesky demonstrates partial open source, some community input, and real-world adoption, but its VC-backed LLC structure, limited community ownership, and lack of clear focus on underserved populations or environmental sustainability constrain its score under this constitution.

Channel.org shows nonprofit structure, participatory democracy aims, and open source code, but lacks evidence of real-world user adoption, community governance, or adapted design for underserved populations in the dossier.

While the project is nonprofit, serves the charity sector, and is in active use, it lacks evidence of participatory governance, open source or open data, and direct service to marginalized communities, resulting in a middling score under this constitution.

CharmVerse offers collaborative tools for web3 communities and participatory democracy, but its for-profit, VC-backed LLC structure, partial open source, and primary service to professional web3 users rather than underserved populations limit its alignment with David Powell's governance- and justice-centered criteria.

Choose a License provides widely used open source infrastructure with some community contribution, but is governed by a for-profit (GitHub), lacks evidence of deep community ownership, and does not directly serve marginalized or underserved populations.

Citizen OS demonstrates strong nonprofit governance, open source commitment, real-world adoption in Estonian government, and a collaborative participatory democracy focus, though its reach beyond Estonia and accessibility for marginalized users are somewhat limited.

Fundación Ciudadanía Inteligente demonstrates strong nonprofit governance, sustained real-world adoption across Latin America, a participatory democracy focus serving citizens and civil society, partial but meaningful open source, and explicit climate and accountability tools, aligning closely with the evaluative constitution's priorities.

CiviClick is a for-profit LLC serving primarily professional advocacy users with no evidence of community governance, open source, or adaptation for underserved populations, and while it supports advocacy infrastructure, it lacks transparency, user-centred design for marginalized groups, and public health or environmental features.
